claim: Information is carried in the brain by the joint spiking patterns of large groups of noisy, unreliable neurons.
source: Information is carried in the brain by the joint spiking patterns of large groups of noisy, unreliable neurons.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established understanding in neuroscience.

claim: Noise limits the capacity of the neural code and determines how information can be transmitted and read-out.
source: This noise limits the capacity of the neural code and determines how information can be transmitted and read-out.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established concepts in information theory and neuroscience.

claim: The brain must overcome noise to accurately decode and identify which patterns are semantically similar.
source: To accurately decode, the brain must overcome this noise and identify which patterns are semantically similar.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the problem of noisy neural coding.

claim: Models of network encoding noise can be used to learn a thesaurus for populations of neurons in the vertebrate retina.
source: We use models of network encoding noise to learn a thesaurus for populations of neurons in the vertebrate retina responding to artificial and natural videos, measuring the similarity between population responses to visual stimuli based on the information they carry.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The neural code is organized in clusters of synonymous activity patterns that are similar in meaning but may differ considerably in their structure.
source: This thesaurus reveals that the code is organized in clusters of synonymous activity patterns that are similar in meaning but may differ considerably in their structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data analysis.

claim: The organization of the neural code is highly reminiscent of the design of engineered codes.
source: This organization is highly reminiscent of the design of engineered codes.
evidence: This is an interpretive comparison drawn from the observed data structure.

claim: The clustered structure of the code allows accurate decoding of novel stimuli from novel spiking patterns.
source: We suggest that the brain may use this structure and show how it allows accurate decoding of novel stimuli from novel spiking patterns.
evidence: This is demonstrated through decoding analysis in the study.

claim: Noise is prevalent in the nervous system from ion channels through synapses and single neurons up to the system level.
source: Noise is prevalent in the nervous system, from ion channels through synapses and single neurons, and up to the system level (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995; Schneidman et al., 1998; Rieke et al., 1999; Osborne et al., 2005; Faisal et al., 2008; Ala-Laurila et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Even when presented with identical stimuli, the brain may receive different spiking patterns from sensory neurons.
source: Consequently, even when presented with identical stimuli, the brain may receive different spiking patterns from the sensory neurons (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995; Berry et al., 1997; de Ruyter van Steveninck et al., 1997; Reich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies demonstrating neural variability.

claim: The nature of neural noise determines how information is encoded in the brain.
source: The nature of neural noise thus determines how information is encoded in the brain (Borst and Theunissen, 1999; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010; Rolls and Treves, 2011), and how it might be read out from neural activity (Warland et al., 1997; Dan et al., 1998; Vargas-Irwin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: In engineering, codes are designed to solve noise problems by choosing codewords that are far apart in the space of patterns relative to typical noise levels.
source: In engineering, codes are designed to solve this problem by choosing codewords that are far apart in the space of patterns, relative to the typical noise levels. That way, if noise corrupts a message, it would still be easily distinguishable from the noisy variants of other codewords (Cover and Thomas, 1991; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011; Curto et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes established principles from information theory and coding theory, supported by citations.

claim: The nature of correlations among neurons is central in shaping the code's capacity and content, particularly in the context of noise.
source: It is clear that the nature of correlations among neurons is central in shaping the code's capacity and content, in particular in the context of noise (Zohary et al., 1994; Zemel et al., 1998; Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Diesmann et al., 1999; Sompolinsky et al., 2001; Schneidman et al., 2006; Pillow et al., 2008; Shlens et al., 2009; Ganmor et al., 2011b; Schwartz et al., 2012; Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research on neural correlations.

claim: The functional role of correlations in encoding information by large populations has been heavily debated.
source: However, the functional role of these correlations in encoding information by large populations has been heavily debated (Nirenberg et al., 2001; Amari et al., 2003; Pola et al., 2003; Schneidman et al., 2003a, 2006; Averbeck et al., 2006; Tkacik et al., 2006; de la Rocha et al., 2007; Pillow et al., 2008; Ecker et al., 2010; Ohiorhenuan et al., 2010; Oizumi et al., 2010; Ganmor et al., 2011a), partly because of the difficulty to study them directly at the network level and the limitations of generalizing from small groups of cells to large ones.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies with differing perspectives.

claim: Semantic similarity between neural activity patterns can be measured by comparing what each pattern tells the brain about the stimulus.
source: We suggest here that the semantic similarity between neural activity patterns can be measured by comparing what each pattern tells the brain about the stimulus.
evidence: This is the core methodological proposal of the study.

claim: Isolated salamander retinas were presented with over 600 repeats of the same 10 s long video clips.
source: To study the variability, or noise, which is inherent to encoding of sensory stimuli by large populations of neurons, we presented isolated salamander retinas with over 600 repeats of the same 10 s long video clips (one natural video and one artificial spatially uniform and temporally Gaussian flicker video), and recorded the joint response of dozens of retinal ganglion cells (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: Each video was presented continuously in a loop for approximately 2 hours.
source: Each video was presented continuously in a loop for ∼2 hr.
evidence: This is a specific experimental parameter.

claim: Single neurons show stochastic, noisy responses to the same stimulus segment.
source: Figure 1A shows examples of the stochastic, or noisy, responses of single neurons from the population to the same stimulus segment (see also Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995; Berry et al., 1997).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: The population activity pattern r(t) is defined as the binary vector of the instantaneous states of each neuron.
source: In order to examine the responses at the population level, we defined the population activity pattern r(t) as the binary vector of the instantaneous states of each neuron: the ith entry in the vector, ri, being 1 if the ith neuron spiked, and 0 if it was silent (responses were binned in 20 ms bins; for other bin sizes see Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the data representation method used in the analysis.

claim: Responses were binned in 20 ms bins.
source: responses were binned in 20 ms bins; for other bin sizes see Figure 5—figure supplement 4
evidence: This is a specific methodological parameter.

claim: The variability of the population responses is high when the population's firing rate goes up.
source: Figure 1C shows the entropy of P(r|s) as a function of time (or, equivalently, of stimulus), along with the instantaneous population rate, reflecting that the variability of the population responses is high when the population's firing rate goes up.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Two neural activity patterns are similar in terms of their meaning to the extent that they convey similar information to the brain.
source: We submit that two neural activity patterns are similar, in terms of their meaning, to the extent that they convey similar information to the brain.
evidence: This is a conceptual definition proposed by the authors.

claim: The meaning of a neural activity pattern r is given by the probability distribution over stimuli conditioned on that response, P(s|r).
source: The meaning of a neural activity pattern r is given by what it tells the brain about its corresponding input, or in the case of sensory systems, the potential stimuli that could have resulted in that response. Since the mapping between stimulus and response is probabilistic, the meaning of r is given by the probability distribution over stimuli conditioned on that response, namely P(s|r).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework based on Bayesian inference.

claim: The experimental design allowed drawing hundreds of samples from P(r|s) for every stimulus s.
source: Our experimental design, in which we presented many repeats of the same video, allowed us to draw hundreds of samples from P(r|s), for every s.
evidence: This describes the advantage of the experimental design.

claim: Due to the exponential number of possible population activity patterns, one cannot directly sample the full distribution even for groups of 20 neurons.
source: However, due to the exponential number of possible population activity patterns one cannot directly sample this distribution in full even for groups of 20 neurons.
evidence: This is a mathematical constraint based on combinatorics.

claim: Average noise correlations for pairs of neurons are typically weak.
source: For pairs of neurons, average noise correlations are typically weak (Cafaro and Rieke, 2010; Ecker et al., 2010), implying that pairs of neurons are not far from being conditionally independent given the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Weak pairwise correlations do not imply that large groups are conditionally independent in encoding stimuli.
source: However, weak pairwise correlations do not imply that large groups are conditionally independent in encoding stimuli (Schneidman et al., 2006; Pillow et al., 2008; Vidne et al., 2012; Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Most stimuli did not evoke a substantial response from the retina, giving rise to low noise correlation in the network for these stimuli.
source: We found that most stimuli did not evoke a substantial response from the retina, which gave rise to low noise correlation in the network for these stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: When something interesting happened in the video and ganglion cells increased their firing rates, there was a sharp increase in network noise correlations for both natural and artificial videos.
source: However, when something 'interesting' happened in the video and the ganglion cells increased their firing rates, we found a sharp increase in the degree of network noise correlations for both natural and artificial videos (Figure 2A,B; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for analysis of sampling properties).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For interesting stimuli, the population was strongly correlated and far from conditionally independent.
source: Thus, while on average the network noise correlations may be weak, the population was strongly correlated and far from conditionally independent in response to interesting stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: For interesting stimuli, the variability or noise at the network level is significantly reduced compared to what would be expected from the apparent noise level of individual cells.
source: In other words, for these stimuli, the variability or noise at the level of the network is significantly reduced compared to what would be expected from the apparent noise level of individual cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the noise correlation findings.

claim: Conditionally independent models of population encoding fail at interesting stimuli.
source: Indeed, conditionally independent models of population encoding (which assume no noise correlations) fail exactly at such interesting stimuli (Pillow et al., 2008; Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013), reflecting that in order to accurately characterize the population responses and the noise, we need a model that takes into account correlations between the cells that depend on the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is consistent with the observed data.

claim: A stimulus-dependent pairwise maximum entropy model was fit for each stimulus to capture firing rates and pairwise noise correlations.
source: We extended the framework of maximum entropy models for neural activity patterns (Schneidman et al., 2006; Shlens et al., 2009), to the population responses to each stimulus (Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013): for each stimulus, s, we fit the minimal model that has the same stimulus dependent firing rates and pairwise noise correlations observed over the repeats of that stimulus.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The pairwise maximum entropy model P(2)(r|s) gave relatively accurate models of the distribution of patterns that the population displayed across repeats for different stimuli.
source: We found that P(2)(r|s) gave relatively accurate models of the distribution of patterns that the population displayed across repeats, for the different stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in agreement with Granot-Atedgi et al. (2013).
evidence: This is a finding from model validation, supported by figure and citation.

claim: The pairwise maximum entropy models captured accurately the strong network noise correlations.
source: In particular, they captured accurately the strong network noise correlations (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Similar spike counts do not imply similar meaning in neural responses.
source: The lack of structure in the matrices for both artificial and natural stimuli shows that similar spike counts do not imply similar meaning.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis of similarity matrices in Figure 3A.

claim: When using hierarchical clustering on the semantic similarity matrices, the population code is arranged in sets or clusters of highly similar activity patterns that are very different from all other patterns.
source: In clear contrast, when we used a hierarchical clustering algorithm on d(ri,rj) matrices and grouped responses together according to their similarity (see 'Materials and methods'), we found that the ordered matrices exhibit an almost perfect block diagonal structure (Figure 3B; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for statistical analysis). Thus, the population code that is used by the retina both for artificial videos, and for natural videos, is arranged in sets, or clusters, of highly similar activity patterns, which are very different from all other patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The Hamming distance does not reveal the clustered structure of the population codebook as effectively as the semantic similarity measure.
source: We examined whether the Hamming distance, which is a simple and intuitive measure of similarity between population responses (the number of neurons that differ in their spiking or silence state), was sufficient to reveal the structure of the population codebook. We thus constructed the matrices of Hamming distances between all pairs of population activity patterns, and clustered the responses, using the same hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Figure 3C shows the Hamming matrix for the same group of 20 cells from a–d, where matrix rows (and columns) are ordered according to the clustering results. We did not find evident structure in the codebook used for natural stimuli, and only slightly more structure was apparent for the artificial stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Measuring similarity in meaning rather than similarity in structure is important for uncovering the clustered organization of the neural population code.
source: These results reflect the importance of measuring similarity in meaning and not similarity in structure. Using a syntactic (structure based) measure, we would not have been able to uncover the clustered organization of the neural population code that the semantic similarity reveals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different similarity measures.

claim: Patterns that belong to the same cluster exhibit some shared structure, with some neurons almost always firing and others always silent.
source: Patterns that belong to the same cluster do exhibit some shared structure, namely some of the neurons almost always fire in a specific cluster and others are always silent (Figure 3B, bottom).
evidence: This is observed in the detailed view of clusters in Figure 3B.

claim: The semantic similarity structure over all patterns could not be captured by a simple linear or bilinear function of the population patterns.
source: However, importantly, we found that the semantic similarity structure over all the patterns we observed could not be captured by a simple linear or bilinear function of the population patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Responses to repeated presentations of a stimulus should come from the same cluster.
source: This gives rise to two important predictions, which we confirmed by cross-validation, using novel (held out) test stimuli: 1. Responses to repeated presentations of a stimulus should come from the same cluster.
evidence: This is a prediction that was tested and confirmed with cross-validation.

claim: Responses from the same cluster should be nearly interchangeable.
source: 2. Responses from the same cluster should be nearly interchangeable.
evidence: This is a prediction that was tested and confirmed with cross-validation.

claim: Even when the most frequent population pattern appeared less than 20% of the time, often over 70% of the observed responses would fall within a single cluster.
source: Notably, even when the population response was highly unreliable (i.e., the most frequent response pattern appeared less than 20% of the time), often over 70% of the observed responses would fall within a single cluster (mostly for the natural video), for the cross-validated test data (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for statistical analysis).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Approximately 100 clusters were enough to account for over 80% of the information available about the stimulus in the detailed population patterns for both types of stimuli.
source: We found that ∼100 clusters were enough to account for over 80% of the information available about the stimulus in the detailed population patterns, for both types of stimuli.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the information analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Clustering the responses based on the Hamming distance gave significantly worse results than semantic similarity clustering.
source: Importantly, clustering the responses based on the Hamming distance between them gave significantly worse results.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 comparing different clustering approaches.

claim: Responses in the same cluster have a similar meaning and can be viewed as noisy variants of a noise-free codeword.
source: This clearly reflects that responses in the same cluster have a similar meaning and can indeed be viewed as noisy variants of a noise-free codeword, similar to the ground states or attractors in a Hopfield model (Hopfield, 1982; Tkacik et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the information analysis results, supported by analogy to known models.

claim: The similarity measure learned from training data predicts stimulus similarity in test data.
source: We find that response similarity measured from the training data predicts stimulus similarity in the test data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows the correlation between cluster similarity and stimulus similarity; for more accurate metrics on stimulus space, see [Tkačik et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 and its supplement.

claim: The similarity between neural responses captures similarity in meaning and generalizes across stimuli.
source: Thus, the similarity measure proposed here for the population responses captures similarity in meaning and generalizes across stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the generalization analysis.

claim: P(s|r) for a held-out test response r could be well estimated by taking P(s|r′) for the response r′ which is most similar to it.
source: Indeed, we found that P(s|r) for a held-out test response, r, could be well estimated simply by taking P(s|r′) for the response, r′, which is most similar to it. Similarity was assessed using the thesaurus that we learned from the training data, that is, for different stimuli than the ones we tested on (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Using a thesaurus based on semantic similarity clearly improved the ability to estimate the stimulus compared to prior knowledge about the stimulus.
source: This approach clearly improved our ability to estimate the stimulus compared to our prior knowledge about the stimulus, as measured by the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the 'true' P(s|r) and the estimate (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7C.

claim: Using a thesaurus based on the Hamming distance clearly degraded performance and reduced the accuracy of the stimulus estimate.
source: Using a thesaurus based on the Hamming distance clearly degraded performance and reduced the accuracy of the stimulus estimate (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Using a very limited set of known responses it is possible to decode novel responses to novel stimuli.
source: Thus, using a very limited set of known responses it is possible to decode novel responses to novel stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the decoding analysis.

claim: The thesaurus may be crucial when encountering new responses to known stimuli due to sensory noise or when generalizing prior knowledge to novel stimuli.
source: This may be crucial when encountering new responses to known stimuli, due to sensory noise, or when generalizing prior knowledge to novel stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: The neural code of the brain is very different from usual mathematical intuition about similarity.
source: Indeed, it revealed that the neural code of the brain is very different than our usual mathematical intuition: what we may regard as intuitive measures, like the Hamming distance, fail to capture the similarity between neural population responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different similarity measures.

claim: The neural population codebook is organized into a relatively small number of semantically different clusters.
source: This organization of the neural population codebook into a relatively small number of semantically different clusters is reminiscent of the design of engineered codes used in communication.
evidence: This is an interpretive comparison based on the observed structure.

claim: Most of the information that the population encodes is held by the identity of the cluster that a specific activity pattern belongs to.
source: Our thesaurus revealed that most of the information that the population encodes is held by the identity of the cluster that a specific activity pattern belongs to, and that more detailed information may be carried by the fine structure of the pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the information analysis.

claim: The analysis reveals a design principle of the population codebook of a sensory circuit.
source: We thus suggest that our analysis reveals a design principle of the population codebook of a sensory circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: For a large neural population, most network activity patterns are observed at most once.
source: We note that for a large neural population, most network activity patterns are observed at most once (Ganmor et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The brain frequently receives from its sensory neurons activity patterns that were never seen before.
source: Thus, the brain frequently receives from its sensory neurons activity patterns that were never seen before.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous claim about pattern rarity.

claim: A semantic similarity measure between neural population responses may explain how novel inputs may be deciphered.
source: In either case, a semantic similarity measure between neural population responses may explain how these novel inputs may be deciphered: when a novel response pattern is encountered it can take on the information content of similar responses, whose meaning is already known.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of the thesaurus.

claim: The thesaurus may explain how sensory noise can be overcome and how the brain can generalize across stimuli.
source: Therefore, the thesaurus may not only explain how sensory noise can be overcome but also how the brain can generalize across stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications.

claim: Uncovering the structure and organization of the population code relied on the ability to accurately model the noisy nature of the population response to specific stimuli.
source: Uncovering the structure and organization of the population code relied on our ability to accurately model the noisy nature of the population response to specific stimuli.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion about what enabled the findings.

claim: Pairwise maximum entropy models were used to capture the noise correlations at every time point.
source: Here, we used pairwise maximum entropy models to capture the 'noise correlations' at every time point, (Figure 2), which were weak on average, but significant at specific times, as was also shown in (Kohn and Smith, 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010; Granot-Atedgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and is supported by citations.

claim: Learning a thesaurus using the conditionally independent model of neural responses recovered a similarity structure that was on par with that revealed by the pairwise model in terms of information about the stimulus.
source: Interestingly, learning a thesaurus using the conditionally independent model of the neural responses to the stimuli, recovered a similarity structure that was on par with that revealed by the pairwise model, in terms of the information that the clusters carried about the stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different models, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The organization of the codebook may be so robust that even an inaccurate model can capture the identity of clusters because the errors of the model are smaller than the distance between clusters.
source: One possible explanation is that the organization of the codebook may be so robust, namely that the separation between clusters is sufficiently large, that even an inaccurate model can capture the identity clusters because the errors of the model are smaller than the distance between clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the robustness finding.

claim: The pairwise models gave better results for decoding stimuli over the conditionally independent model.
source: Finally, we note again that the pairwise models gave better results for decoding stimuli over the conditionally independent model.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: The semantic similarity between population responses could not be approximated by simple linear or bilinear functions of the patterns.
source: But maybe most importantly, we found that the semantic similarity between population responses could not be approximated by simple linear or bilinear functions of the patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from attempting to fit simpler models.

claim: Noise showed a high degree of stimulus dependence.
source: This is mostly due to the fact that noise showed a high degree of stimulus dependence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlated nature of neural noise shapes the population code differently for different stimuli.
source: This means that the correlated nature of neural noise shapes the population code differently for different stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stimulus-dependent noise findings.

claim: Experiments were performed on the adult tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum).
source: Experiments were performed on the adult tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: All experiments were approved by the institutional animal care and use committee of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and were in accordance with government regulations.
source: All experiments were approved by the institutional animal care and use committee of Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and were in accordance with government regulations.
evidence: This is an ethical compliance statement.

claim: 48/31 retinal ganglion cells were recorded and cleanly isolated in the artificial/natural video experiment.
source: 48/31 retinal ganglion cells were recorded and cleanly isolated in the artificial/natural video experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data.

claim: Natural video clips were acquired using a digital video camera at 30 frames per second.
source: Natural video clips were acquired using a digital video camera (Sony Handycam DCR-HC23) at 30 frames per second.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: The stimulus was projected onto the salamander retina from a CRT video monitor at a frame rate of 60 Hz.
source: The stimulus was projected onto the salamander retina from a CRT video monitor (ViewSonic G90fB) at a frame rate of 60 Hz such that each acquired frame was presented twice, using standard optics (Puchalla et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citation.

claim: Ten randomly chosen groups of 20 neurons from each retina were examined.
source: We examined the responses of ten randomly chosen groups of 20 neurons from each retina.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data analysis.

claim: The multi-information I(r|s) was used to quantify the correlation of the population in encoding stimulus s.
source: Specifically, we quantified the correlation of the population in encoding the stimulus s, by the multi-information, I(r|s)=H[Pind (r|s)]−H[P(r|s)] (Amari, 2001; Schneidman et al., 2003b), where H[Pind (r|s)] is the entropy assuming neurons are independent given the stimulus—Pind(r|s)=ΠiP(ri|s), and H[P(r|s)] is the entropy of the joint population response to the stimulus s (estimated following Strong et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes the mathematical measure used, with citations.

claim: The multi-information I(r|s) measures the total correlations of all orders among the cells.
source: We note that I(r|s) measures the total correlations of all orders among the cells.
evidence: This is a clarification of what the measure captures.
